1.pericope_label: We do you to wit of the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia; their deep poverty abounded

schools.summary: Calvin explains the placing of the appeal. In the event of the Corinthians retaining any feeling of offence occasioned by the severity of the preceding Epistle, which might stand in the way of Paul's authority having influence over them, he has hitherto made it his endeavour to conciliate their affections; and now, after clearing away all occasion of offence and regaining favour for his ministry, he recommends to them the brethren at Jerusalem, that they may furnish help to their necessities. He could not with any great advantage have attempted this at the commencement of the Epistle, and has therefore prudently deferred it until he has prepared their minds for it — taking up the whole of this chapter and the next in exhorting them to be active and diligent in collecting alms, since the brethren were afflicted with a great famine and could scarcely support life without being aided by other churches. On the Macedonians' joy Calvin observes that while they were tried with adversity they nevertheless did not cease to rejoice in the Lord, and that this disposition rose so high as to swallow up sorrow, since their minds, which must otherwise have been straitened, required to be set free from their restraints that they might liberally furnish aid to the brethren. By joy he means that spiritual consolation by which believers are sustained under their afflictions, and he distinguishes it sharply from its counterfeits: the wicked either delude themselves with empty consolations, avoiding a perception of the evil and drawing off the mind to rambling thoughts, or else wholly give way to grief and allow themselves to be overwhelmed by it, whereas believers seek occasions of joy in the affliction itself. Gill sets out the occasion in the same way, that the apostle, having said everything proper to conciliate the minds and affections of the Corinthians, and the matter in difference being adjusted to the satisfaction of all parties, now proposes what he had wisely postponed till all was over; and he glosses the obsolete phrase, that to do one to wit is to acquaint with, inform of, or give knowledge of anything. Of the Macedonians' condition Gill notes that they received the Gospel at first in much affliction, as did the church at Thessalonica, and afterwards suffered much from their countrymen by reproaches, persecutions, imprisonments and confiscation of goods; and he draws the comparison that gives the passage its force — for persons in prosperity, when all things go well with them, to be liberal is no such great matter, but for persons in adversity, under trying dispensations of Providence, to communicate generously to the relief of others is something very remarkable, and worthy of notice and imitation.

Barnes explains what makes the Macedonian gift remarkable: it came when it might be supposed they were unable to give, when many would suppose they themselves needed the aid of others, and when their minds might have been wholly engrossed with their own concerns — the trial referred to being doubtless some persecution excited against them, probably by the Jews. Their joy, arising from the hopes and promises of the gospel, could not be repressed by their persecution, and the effect of it was seen in the liberal contribution they made. Ellicott would render the opening verb simply we declare or make known, there being no adequate reason for retaining a phrase now obsolete, and finds something intensely characteristic in the way the Apostle opens his statement by tracing the generosity of the Macedonians to its true source. He notes that the churches of Macedonia, Philippi prominent among them, had been true to their old generosity, showing it now not in personal kindness to their teacher but in the truer way of acting as he wished, so that the Apostle sees in it a means of stirring up his friends at Corinth to an honourable emulation. On the affliction Ellicott admits we do not know what is specially referred to, but observes that a community of Christians in a heathen city was always exposed to trials of this kind, and that the temper shown by the rulers at Philippi and the Jews of Thessalonica makes it almost certain that they would carry on at least a petty persecution. He offers two accounts of the poverty: that at Philippi may possibly be connected with the preponderance of women in the church there, since in the absence of the bread-winners of a household Christian women in a Graeco-Roman city would find but scanty means of subsistence; and in part the churches were sharers in a widely spread distress, Macedonia and Achaia having never recovered from the three civil wars, so that under Tiberius they petitioned for a diminution of their burdens. Robertson supplies the historical note that the Romans had lacerated Macedonia, and glosses the phrase for their want as poverty down deep, comparing Strabo's use of the same expression for down to the bottom; on the word rendered liberality he reports Plummer's remark that the passage from single-mindedness or simplicity to liberality is not quite obvious, and suggests that heartiness may supply the connecting link.

Henry takes the Apostle to be using the good example of the churches of Macedonia — Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea and others in that region — to exhort the Corinthians and the Christians of Achaia to the good work of charity. He acquaints them with their great liberality, which he calls the grace of God bestowed on the churches, though Henry notes that some think the words should be rendered the gift of God given in or by the churches. He certainly means the charitable gifts of these churches, which are called the grace or gifts of God either because they were very large, or rather because their charity to the poor saints proceeded from God as the author and was accompanied with true love to God, which was manifested this way. From this Henry draws his rule: the grace of God must be owned as the root and fountain of all the good that is in us, or done by us, at any time, and it is great grace and favour from God, and bestowed on us, if we are made useful to others and are forward in every good work.

Clarke states the paradox of the passage as a rule about comparative terms: the Macedonians, though both poor and persecuted, rejoiced exceedingly that an opportunity was afforded them of doing good to their more impoverished and more persecuted brethren. We can scarcely ever speak of poverty and affliction in an absolute sense, he says, since they are only comparative — even the poor are called to relieve those who are poorer than themselves, and the afflicted to comfort those who are more afflicted than they are; and the poor and afflicted churches of Macedonia felt this duty, and therefore came forward to the uttermost of their power to relieve their more impoverished and afflicted brethren in Judea. Wesley states both halves of the verse in short compass, that the grace of God evidently appeared by this happy effect, and that the great trial of affliction consisted in their being continually persecuted, harassed and plundered.

3.pericope_label: To their power, and beyond their power, they were willing of themselves, praying us with much intreaty

schools.summary: Barnes takes the phrase beyond their power to mean beyond what could have been expected, or beyond what it would have been thought possible in their condition, the sense being that they were willing to give more than they were well able; and he notes that Paul, having founded those churches and spent much time with them, was well qualified to bear testimony in regard to their condition. He passes on Doddridge's remark that this is a noble hyperbole, similar to that used by Demosthenes when he said that he had performed all, even with an industry beyond his power. On the entreaty Barnes explains that they were earnestly begging the Apostle to receive the contribution and convey it to the poor and afflicted saints in Judea, and takes the occasion of the distress to have been probably the famine predicted by Agabus, which occurred in the time of Claudius Caesar. On the fifth verse he draws the explanation of the whole: they first made an entire consecration of themselves and all they had to the Lord, keeping nothing back and feeling that all they had was his — and where a people honestly and truly devote themselves to God, they will find no difficulty in having the means to contribute. Ellicott renders the phrase for their willingness as literally spontaneously, and identifies this as the point of excellence the Apostle wished to hold up as an example, since those of Macedonia needed no appeal or counsel such as he had given to the Corinthians and to others. On the entreaty he corrects the received text, since the words that we would receive are not in the Greek, which runs literally, asking of us the grace, or favour, and fellowship in the ministry of the saints — that is, asking to be allowed to share in it. On the giving of themselves he notes that they gave not their money only, but themselves, their time, thought and energy, primarily to Christ as their Lord and then to the Apostle as his minister, and that they did so because they allowed the will of God to work upon their will. On the sending of Titus Ellicott reconstructs the sequence, that when Titus came to Corinth he had begun to take measures for this collection and had been to a certain extent successful, and that it was the report of that success which encouraged Paul to entreat him to return and bring the good work to completion. Robertson supplies the prepositions, that the phrase means alongside or past their ability, and reports that Field quotes Josephus for the same pair of expressions; few, he observes, give even according to actual ability, and Paul commends this high-pressure collection because of the emergency. He glosses the word for of their own accord as an old verbal adjective meaning of their own initiative, voluntary, found only here and later in this chapter in the New Testament, and notes that the papyri often pair it with the word for willingly. On the entreaty he observes that the accusative after the verb of begging is unusual, that by grace Paul means the privilege of giving, and that apparently the Apostle had been reluctant to press the Macedonians because of their manifest poverty, so that they demanded the right to have a share in it. On the fifth verse Robertson puts the explanation most compactly: themselves they gave first, and that is the explanation of the generous giving.

Clarke states the Macedonian rule of giving: in their liberality they had no rule but their ability, believing they were bound to contribute all they could — and even this rule they transgressed, for they went beyond their power, depriving themselves for a time of the necessaries of life in order to give to others who were destitute even of necessaries. On the entreaty he notes that the apostles had not to solicit them to this great act of kindness, since they even entreated to have their bounty accepted and to have the administration or application of it taken upon the apostles' hands. On the fifth verse Clarke says they far exceeded expectation, consecrating themselves entirely to the work of God, giving themselves and all they possessed first unto the Lord, and then, as they saw it was the will of God that they should come forward in this charitable work, giving themselves to the apostles to assist to the uttermost in providing relief for the suffering Christians in Judea. On the sending of Titus he adds that Titus had probably laid the plan of this contribution when he was before at Corinth, according to the direction the Apostle had given in the earlier letter. Wesley supposes that Paul had lovingly admonished the Macedonians not to give beyond their power, which explains what they were entreating against; and on their giving of themselves he glosses the phrase as meaning that they gave themselves to the apostles in obedience to the will of God, to be wholly directed by them.

Calvin enlarges on the Macedonians' promptitude, since they did not merely refrain from waiting for anyone to admonish them, but anticipated by their activity the desires of those by whom they would have been admonished; and he presses the comparison between the less and the greater which governs the whole chapter — if the Macedonians, without needing to be besought, press forward of their own accord, and go further and anticipate others by using entreaties, the Corinthians have something to be ashamed of. On their giving of themselves he raises the question whether their giving themselves to God and to Paul were two different things, and answers that it is quite a common thing that when God charges or commands through means of any one, he associates the person whom he employs as his minister both in the authority to enjoin and in the obedience that is rendered. Gill notes that they gave according to their ability, to the utmost of it, which is the most that can be desired or given, since no man can give more than he has nor is required to do more than he is able; that they not only gave freely, being unasked by the apostles, but sought to them and earnestly entreated them; and that all this was unexpected by the apostles, who knew their great affliction and deep poverty and could not have hoped for such a collection from them.

7.pericope_label: As ye abound in every thing, see that ye abound in this grace also; I speak not by commandment

schools.summary: Chrysostom hears the exhortation accompanied with commendations, and greater commendations than before, and marks the Apostle's choice of verb: he said not that ye give, but that ye abound — in faith, meaning of the gifts; in utterance, the word of wisdom; in knowledge, that is of the doctrines; and in all earnestness, to the attaining of all other virtue; and in your love, that of which he had spoken before and of which he had made proof. For this reason, Chrysostom says, the Apostle began with those praises, that advancing forward he might draw them on to the same diligence in these things also. On the verse that follows he observes how constantly Paul humours them, how he avoids offensiveness, and how he is neither violent nor compulsory.

Barnes observes that Paul never hesitated to commend Christians where it could be done with truth, and that the fact of their being eminent in some of the Christian duties and graces is made the ground of an exhortation that they should abound in all: from those who had so many characteristics of true religion he had a right to expect much, and he therefore exhorts them to manifest a symmetry of Christian character. He glosses the items — faith as the full belief of the truth and obligation of the gospel, utterance as the ability to instruct others, perhaps referring to their power of speaking foreign languages, and knowledge as the knowledge of God and of his truth. On the disclaimer that follows Barnes explains that it does not mean the Apostle had no express command of God in the case, but that he did not mean to command them or to speak authoritatively; he used only moral motives, endeavouring to induce them to give liberally not by abstract command and law but by showing them what others had given who had much less ability. Men cannot be induced to give to objects of charity by command, or by a spirit of dictation and authority, Barnes adds; the only successful, as well as the only lawful, appeal is to their hearts. Ellicott notes the particle that marks the transition from narrative to exhortation, and observes how dexterously the Apostle combines the gifts of utterance and knowledge which he had acknowledged in the earlier letter with the earnestness and love of which he had spoken in this one. On the last item he prefers the received reading, your love to us, against the manuscripts which give our love for you, judging that it has abundant authority and gives a far better meaning, and finding a subtle delicacy in the Greek — the love which, flowing from them, rests in the Apostle as its object. On the disclaimer he states the ambiguity plainly: the English, and indeed the Greek also, leaves us uncertain whether the Apostle disclaims merely the tone of command or the sanction of a divine authority, the former seeming preferable, though ultimately the one runs into the other, since he gives no commands in this matter because he has received no commandment from the Lord himself. Robertson makes the sharpest observation on the opening praise, that this gifted church had fallen behind in the grace of giving, and that there is kindly irony in the allusion; and on the following verse he glosses the participle as testing and so proving, and the word rendered sincerity as an old adjective meaning legitimately born rather than spurious — a collection being a test of one's love for Christ, not the only test, but a real one.

Calvin notes how careful the Apostle has been to avoid giving offence, having said that Titus entreated them not so much from his own inclination as in consideration of the charge given him by the Macedonians; and now he goes a step farther, admonishing them that they must not even wait for the message of the Macedonians to be communicated to them — and doing it by commending their other virtues, as if to say that they ought not merely to associate themselves as partners with the Macedonians but to surpass them in this respect as they do in others. On the disclaimer Calvin says the Apostle qualifies his exhortation by declaring that he did not at all intend to compel them, as if imposing any necessity, for that is what is done when we enjoin anything definite and peremptorily require that it be done. Should any one ask whether it was not lawful for him to prescribe what he had by commandment of the Lord, the answer is easy: God, it is true, everywhere charges us to help the necessities of our brethren, but he nowhere specifies the sum, so that after making a calculation we might divide between ourselves and the poor, and he nowhere binds us to circumstances of times or of persons, but calls us to take the rule of love as our guide. Gill states the same refusal in practical terms: the Apostle did not speak in a peremptory manner, extorting from them a collection or laying his apostolical injunctions upon them to make one, and did not go about to force or oblige them to it, for men in such cases must act willingly, and what they do they must do of their own accord and with cheerfulness, not through constraint or grudgingly. God, he adds, has not fixed the certain times when, or the certain sums which, persons are to give, but has signified in general that those in necessity are to be relieved by such as are in ability to do it.

Henry treats the opening compliment as strategy, and admires it. Great address and much holy art are here used by the Apostle: when he would persuade the Corinthians to this good thing, he commends them for other good things that were found in them — most people loving to be complimented, especially when we ask a gift of them for ourselves or for others, and it being a justice we owe to those in whom God's grace shines to give them their due commendation. Henry then observes what it was that the Corinthians abounded in, and notes that faith is mentioned first because that is the root from which the rest proceed.

Clarke runs through the list of graces item by item: faith is the crediting of the whole testimony of God; utterance is doctrine, the knowing what to teach; knowledge is of God's will, with prudence to direct them in teaching and doing it; diligence is to amend all that is wrong among them and to do what is right; and love to us means the love with which they now prize the apostles as the apostles of the Lord and their pastors in him. The exhortation, he concludes, is that they should be as eminent for their charitable disposition as they are for faith, doctrine, knowledge, diligence and love. On the disclaimer Clarke says the Apostle does not positively order this and assumes no right or authority over their property, since what they devote of their substance to charitable purposes must be their own work and a free-will offering; and he notes that Paul takes this opportunity to apprise them of the zeal of the Macedonians, lest those at Corinth, who excelled in every other gift, should be outdone in this — their own honour, if better motives were absent, inducing them to exert themselves.

9.pericope_label: Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich

schools.summary: Barnes explains why the Apostle reaches for this argument here: Paul was accustomed to illustrate every subject, and to enforce every duty where it could be done, by a reference to the life and sufferings of the Lord Jesus Christ. The design of the verse is to show the duty of giving liberally to the objects of benevolence, from the fact that the Lord Jesus was willing to become poor in order that he might benefit others — the idea being that he who was Lord and Proprietor of the universe, and who possessed all things, was willing to leave his exalted station in the bosom of the Father and to become poor, in order that we might become rich in the blessings of the gospel, in the means of grace, and as heirs of all things; and that we who are thus benefited, and who have such an example, should be willing to give. Ellicott notices first that the sense of the word grace is slightly modified by the context, the theological sense falling into the background and that of an act of liberality becoming prominent. He would render the participle being rich rather than though he was rich, and finds the thought the same as that expressed in the Philippian hymn, especially in the words which ought to be translated He emptied Himself: he was rich in the ineffable glory of the divine attributes, and these he renounced for a time in the mystery of the Incarnation, taking our nature in all its poverty. That is doubtless the chief thought expressed, Ellicott says, but we can scarcely doubt that the words refer also to the outward aspect of our Lord's life, since he chose the lot of the poor. Robertson marks the tenses: the participle rendered though he was rich is concessive; the verb rendered he became poor is an ingressive aorist, from the same root as the word used of the Macedonians' poverty earlier in the chapter; the phrase through his poverty is instrumental, by means of; and the verb rendered might become rich is likewise an ingressive aorist.

Calvin adduces Christ as an all-perfect and singular pattern of the love the Apostle has just mentioned: though he was rich, he resigned the possession of all blessings, that he might enrich us by his poverty. He notes what the Apostle does not go on to do — he does not afterwards state for what purpose he makes mention of this, but leaves it to be considered by his readers, since no one can fail to perceive that we are by this example stirred up not to spare ourselves when help is to be afforded to our brethren. Calvin then establishes the wealth in two stages: Christ was rich because he was God, under whose power and authority all things are; and further, even in the human nature which he put on, he was heir of all, inasmuch as he was placed by his Father over all creatures and all things were placed under his feet. Gill calls the appeal a new argument and a very forcible one, taken from the wonderful grace and love of Christ displayed in his state of humiliation towards his people, which is well known to all who have truly believed in him; of this they are not and cannot be ignorant, his love and good will and favour being so manifest, and there being such glaring proofs of it in his incarnation, sufferings and death as leave no room for any to doubt.

Clarke calls this the strongest argument of all, and urged home by the Apostle with admirable address: they are acquainted with God's ineffable love in sending Jesus Christ into the world, and they know the grace, the infinite benevolence, of Christ himself. He fills out both terms of the contrast concretely — Christ was the possessor, as he was the creator, of the heavens and the earth, and for their sakes he became poor, emptying himself, making himself of no reputation, taking upon himself the form of a servant, and humbling himself unto death, even the death of the cross; and that through his poverty, that is through his humiliation and death, they might be rich, might regain their forfeited inheritance, and be enriched with every grace of his Holy Spirit. Wesley states the connection between knowing and loving in a clause, that this knowledge is the true source of love; defines the grace as the most sincere, most free and most abundant love; and identifies the two poverties and the riches — that Christ became poor in becoming man, in all his life and in his death, and that the riches which come of it are riches in the favour and image of God.

10.pericope_label: Herein I give my advice: now therefore perform the doing of it, out of that which ye have

schools.summary: Barnes explains the force of the word rendered advice and the reason for choosing it: the Apostle does not undertake to command them, or to prescribe how much they should give, and advice will go much farther than commands on the subject of charities. On the word rendered expedient he says it means that this will be of advantage to them, will be profitable, will be becoming — the idea being that they were bound by a regard to consistency and to their own welfare to perform what they had purposed, since it became them, and there would have been a manifest disadvantage if it had not been done. On the exhortation to finish he presses the point for his own readers: if we have felt it our duty to aid in a cause of benevolence and have commenced it, and have then been interrupted in executing our purpose, we should seize the first favourable opportunity to accomplish what we had designed, not regarding ourselves as released from the obligation but, from a regard to consistency and to our obligation to God, accomplishing what we had intended. Ellicott notes the same careful distinction between command and counsel which appears in the earlier Epistle. On the clause about beginning before he renders it that they got the start, last year, not only as to the doing but also as to the willing, and meets the apparent anti-climax: what is meant is that the Corinthians had been before the Macedonian churches in both those stages, having formed the purpose of giving and having begun to lay by and to collect before their rivals had started — they had, as it were, scored those two points in that game of honourable competition, and it was profitable for them that the Apostle, as a bystander watching the game, should give them a word of encouragement. On the exhortation Ellicott would render it complete the doing rather than perform the doing, and marks the three stages distinctly present in the Apostle's mind: willing the purpose to give, in which they had shown readiness; setting about the work of giving, which Titus had reported; and completing the work, which he now urges upon them, so that it might answer to the beginning. Robertson calls the word a deliberate opinion and not a command, and glosses the two articular infinitives to the effect that the Corinthians promised before any others; on the readiness to will he notes an old word meaning forwardness or eagerness, remarking that they were quick to pledge, and renders the qualifying phrase out of the having, that is, out of what you can give.

Calvin sets the expedient against the commanded, and admits that the judgment of the flesh will not follow him: where is the man to be found who is persuaded that it is expedient to deprive himself of something with the view of helping others? He answers with the saying of a heathen poet, that what you have given away is the only riches you will always have. On the exhortation to finish, Calvin suspects that the ardour of the Corinthians had quickly cooled down, since otherwise they would without any delay have prosecuted their purpose; yet the Apostle, as though no fault had as yet been committed, gently admonishes them to complete what had been well begun. On the qualifying phrase he sees an objection anticipated, for the flesh is always ingenious in finding out subterfuges: some plead that they have families which it were inhuman to neglect, and others, on the ground that they cannot give much, make that a pretext for entire exemption — all which excuses the Apostle removes when he commands every one to contribute according to the measure of his ability. Gill observes that the Apostle did not choose to make use of his apostolical authority or to give orders, as he sometimes did in such cases, looking upon this as the most prudential step and the wisest method he could take in order to succeed — only to give his judgment in the matter, as what would be best for them and most conducive to their real good; and he adds that as it is not enough to do a thing unless it is done cheerfully and willingly, so it is not sufficient to express a good will to such service without doing it, both being required together.

Henry warns against stopping at the purpose. Good purposes are like buds and blossoms, pleasant to behold, and giving hopes of good fruit, but they are lost and signify nothing without good deeds; good beginnings are well, but we lose the benefit unless there is perseverance. He guards the point on both sides: when men purpose that which is good, and endeavour according to their ability to perform also, God will not reject them for what it is not in their power to do — but this scripture will not justify those who think good meanings are enough, or that good purposes and the mere profession of a willing mind are enough to save. He adds the providential observation that lies behind the whole arrangement, that Providence gives to some more of the good things of this world and to some less, so that those who have abundance might supply the wants of others.

Clarke takes the counsel as following from the disclaimer of the previous verse, and states the reason for haste: it is necessary they should do this to preserve a consistency of conduct, for they began the work a year ago and it is necessary that they should complete it as soon as possible. On the disputed clause he takes the difficulty by the word itself — literally it is to do and to will, but since the will must come before the deed, the second word must here be taken in the sense of delight, as it frequently means in both Testaments; and he notes besides that some manuscripts transpose the words, in which case there is no difficulty at all. On the qualifying phrase Clarke answers the excuse it might seem to license: give as God has enabled you, and give as God has disposed you, since he requires each man to do as he can, and accepts the will where the means are wanting to perform the deed.

12.pericope_label: If there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not

schools.summary: Barnes states the rule at its widest: if there is a readiness, a disposition to give, if the heart is in it, then the offering will be acceptable to God whether one be able to give much or little. A willing mind is the first consideration — no donation, however large, can be acceptable where that does not exist, and none, however small, can be otherwise than acceptable where it is found. This had relation, as Paul used it, to the duty of almsgiving, but Barnes notes that the principle is as applicable to everything in the way of duty, a willing mind being the first and main thing, that which God chiefly desires, and that without which everything else will be offensive, hypocritical and vain. On the disclaimer that follows he explains the literal sense, that there should not be rest, a letting loose or remission, to others, but affliction to you; and he supposes the Corinthians were able to contribute more than many other churches, certainly more than the churches of Macedonia, so that Paul presses on them the duty of giving according to their means while by no means intending that the entire burden should come upon them. Ellicott connects the willing mind with the preceding phrase about what they have, and observes that the Apostle is expecting a sum large relatively and not absolutely. He suspects behind the words the history of the widow's mite, found in the Gospel of his friend St. Luke, which was probably not unknown to Paul as belonging to those words of the Lord Jesus which he freely cites; at all events, he has imbibed the spirit of its teaching from other like words. On the disclaimer Ellicott reads it as obviously an answer to something that had been said, since the argument that charity begins at home, with which the workers in the cause of missions and other distant works of charity are but too familiar, would seem not to have been unknown in the Church of Corinth. Robertson glosses the opening verb as lying before one, notes that the second clause has a present indicative rather than a subjunctive because a specific case is presented, and draws the plain conclusion that God clearly does not expect us to give what we do not have; on the disclaimer he supplies the ellipsis, release to others, tribulation to you.

Gill states the measure from the giver's side: if what is done springs from a truly noble, generous spirit, a spirit of bountifulness and liberality, and is given cheerfully and freely and according to a man's ability, the quantity matters not, whether it be more or less. On the disclaimer he sees the balance struck in two directions — within the church, so that the whole burden of the collection should not be put upon some while others were excused doing little or nothing, but everyone should give according to his ability; and between churches, so that those in poorer circumstances should not be entirely freed from the service, as the instance of the Macedonians plainly shows they were not, nor the whole devolved upon the Corinthians and others that were rich. Calvin takes the verse as a confirmation of what precedes, that a readiness of will is well-pleasing to God alike in poverty and in wealth, inasmuch as God does not mean that we should be reduced to straits in order that others may be at ease through our liberality. He adds the qualification a theologian would want: it is certain that we owe to God not merely a part but all that we are and all that we have, yet in his kindness he spares us thus far, that he is satisfied with the participation of which the Apostle here speaks — what is taught here being an abatement from the rigour of law.

Clarke defines what a man has narrowly, taking it of his real property, which means not taking that which belongs to his own family and is indispensably necessary for their support, and not taking that which belongs to others, namely what he owes to any man. On the disclaimer he states the Apostle's meaning in a sentence: I do not design that you should impoverish yourselves in order that others may live affluently. Wesley extends the measure well beyond almsgiving. Every believer is accepted with God according to what he hath, and the same rule holds universally: whoever acknowledges himself to be a vile, guilty sinner, and in consequence of that acknowledgment flies for refuge to the wounds of a crucified Saviour and relies on his merits alone for salvation, may in every circumstance of life apply this indulgent declaration to himself.

14.pericope_label: By an equality, that there may be equality: he that had gathered much had nothing over

schools.summary: Barnes reads the equality as a reciprocity which circumstances may one day reverse. Corinth was then able to give liberally, but many of the other churches were not, being poor and perhaps persecuted and in affliction; yet there might be great reverses in their condition, Corinth being reduced from its affluence and itself becoming dependent on the aid of others, or unable to contribute anything for the purposes of charity — so that the members of the church at Corinth should so act in their circumstances of prosperity that others would be disposed to aid them should reverses come. On the quotation he explains the original setting at length: the manna which fell around the camp of Israel was gathered every morning by all who were able, and when collected it was distributed in the proportion of an omer, about five pints, to each man; some would be more active and more successful than others, some by age or infirmity would collect little, and probably many, being confined to the camp, would collect none — so that those who had gathered more than an omer would in this way contribute to the wants of others. Ellicott states the case plainly, that the Church of Jerusalem was at this time suffering from poverty and the Apostle therefore exhorts the Corinthians to come to its assistance, while a time might come in which their relative position would be inverted, and then he would plead not less earnestly that Jerusalem should assist Corinth. He is the most restrictive of the witnesses about any second sense, judging it to be reading too much between the lines to find here the thought the Apostle expresses elsewhere, that the equality consisted in the Corinthians giving money and receiving spiritual privileges. On the quotation he notes that it follows one of the readings of the Greek version of Exodus, and that the work of love was in the Apostle's thoughts like the manna in the wilderness — in the long run all would be filled, each according to his several necessities. Robertson glosses the word for equality as an old one meaning fair or equal, found in the New Testament only here and in one other place, and the words for abundance and want as late formations.

Calvin admits that it is uncertain what sort of equality the Apostle means, and canvasses the alternatives. Some interpret it as meaning that the Gospel had flowed out to the Corinthians from the Church at Jerusalem, so that in their penury the Jerusalem believers had already assisted them by their spiritual riches — which Calvin thinks foreign to Paul's intention. It ought rather, in his opinion, to be applied to the communion of saints, which means that whatever duty is discharged to one member redounds to the advantage of the entire body; and he puts the argument in the Apostle's mouth, that if it is irksome to help your brethren with riches that are of no value, you should consider how many blessings you are destitute of, and those far more precious, with which you may be enriched by those whom you are asked to help. On the quotation Calvin draws the lesson the manna was given to teach: the Lord would have it serve as a never-failing proof that men do not live by bread alone but are divinely supported, and Moses admonishes them elsewhere that they had been nourished for a time with such food that they might learn that men are supported not by their own industry or labour but by the blessing of God — so that in the manna, as in a mirror, there is presented to us an emblem of the ordinary food that we partake of. Gill keeps to the plainest sense, that all the Apostle meant was that there might be an equality both in givers and in receivers, proportioned to their several circumstances and stations of life.

Clarke turns the equality into a rule of conduct: do to those who are distressed now as, on a change of circumstances, you would wish them to do to you; and he presses the possibility of such a change, since human affairs are so liable to alteration that it is as possible that rich Corinthians should need the charitable help of others as that those Jews, who once had need of nothing, should now be dependent on Corinthian bounty. The aim, he says, is that they should so exert themselves on behalf of those poor people that there may be between them an equality in the necessaries of life, the abundance of the one supplying the want of the other. On the manna Clarke gives the same reconstruction as Barnes with the domestic detail filled in: probably every man gathered as much as he could, and when he brought it home and measured it by the omer, any surplus went to the supply of some other family that had not been able to collect enough, the household being large and the time before the heat of the day insufficient — so that there was an equality among the Israelites. Wesley allows a further meaning beside the temporal one: as the temporal bounty of the Corinthians now supplied the temporal wants of their poor brethren in Judea, so the prayers of these might be a means of bringing down many spiritual blessings on their benefactors, so that all the spiritual wants of the one might be amply supplied and all the temporal wants of the other.

16.pericope_label: Thanks be to God, which put the same earnest care into the heart of Titus; of his own accord he went

schools.summary: Chrysostom explains why the chapter turns from the giving to the men who will carry the gift. Since the Apostle had discoursed of almsgiving, he afterwards discourses also of those who are to receive the money from them and carry it away; for this was of aid towards the collection, and towards increasing the forwardness of the contributors. He that feels confidence as to him who ministers, and suspects not those who are to be receivers, gives with the fuller bountifulness — and that this might be the case then also, Chrysostom says, one should hear how Paul commends those that had come for the purpose, the first of whom was Titus.

Barnes observes that Paul regarded every right feeling, every pure desire, every inclination to serve God or to benefit a fellow-mortal, as the gift of God, and therefore ascribed the praise to him that Titus was disposed to show an interest in the welfare of the Corinthians. The earnest care referred to, he explains, was that the Corinthians might complete the collection and finish what they had proposed, and Titus was willing to undertake this and to see that it was done; the Apostle represents it as being done for them, since although the poor saints in Judea were to have the immediate benefit of the contribution, the Corinthians would have the benefit of the giving. On the following verse Barnes notes that Titus cheerfully complied with the exhortation given him, but that the phrase means more than compliance: he was more disposed to go than the Apostle had supposed, more ready to engage in it than Paul was to exhort him to it, so that he anticipated the request and went voluntarily and without urging. Ellicott corrects the tense, which is present rather than past — who putteth, not who put — referring it to what was then passing after Titus's return from Corinth; and on the phrase the same earnest care he explains that no direct comparison is expressed, but that the care meant is the same as the Apostle's own, Titus having shown himself a true son of his spiritual father. On the following verse he finds the words serving a twofold purpose, both to show that Titus was authorised by the Apostle and acting at his request, and to show that he was so eager to go that he did not even need to be requested; and he notes that the tense of he went is what is known as the epistolary aorist, Titus being probably about to start as the bearer of this very letter. Robertson makes the same grammatical point in fewer words, that the present active articular participle presents God as continually giving, and hence that Titus is full of zealous care for them; and on the comparative in the following verse he glosses it as more earnest than ordinarily.

Calvin observes that the Apostle, in order to leave the Corinthians without excuse, now at length adds that there had been provided for them active prompters who would attend to the matter; and he names Titus first, who, he says, had been divinely raised up. This was of great importance in the case, since the embassy would be so much the more successful if the Corinthians recognised Titus as having come to them from having been stirred up to it by God; and from this passage, as from innumerable others, Calvin infers that there are no pious affections that do not proceed from the Spirit of God, and further that it is an evidence of God's concern for his people that he raises up such men. On the following verse he marks a self-correction in the Apostle's own words: he first says that Titus had undertaken this business from being exhorted to it by Paul, and then corrects it by saying that Titus had not been so much influenced by the advice of others as he had felt stirred up of his own accord, in accordance with his active disposition. Gill introduces the section in the same terms, that the Apostle now gives an account of the persons and their characters who were employed in making this collection at Corinth, beginning with Titus, and the rather because he had already been concerned in setting that good work afoot among them; and he notes that Titus did not refuse but readily accepted the exhortation to go and finish what he had already begun.

Henry describes the whole passage as a set of letters credential. The Apostle commends the brethren who were sent to collect their charity and, as it were, gives them letters credential, so that if they were enquired after, and if any should be inquisitive or suspicious concerning them, it might be known who they were and how safely they might be trusted. He commends Titus on two grounds: for his earnest care and great concern of heart for them, and his desire in all things to promote their welfare, which is mentioned with thankfulness to God — it being cause of thankfulness if God has put it into the hearts of any to do us or others any good; and for his readiness to this present service, since he accepted the office and was forward to undertake it.

Clarke thanks God with the Apostle for having already disposed the heart of Titus to attend to this business, and notes that Paul, with his usual address, considers all this as done on behalf of the Corinthian church — for though the poor Christians in Judea are to have the immediate benefit, God put honour upon the Corinthians in making them his instruments in supplying the wants of others, and he who is an almoner to God Almighty is highly honoured indeed. On the following verse Clarke states the sequence plainly: he advised Titus to visit them and excite them to this good work, and found that he was already disposed in his heart to do it, God having put this earnest care in his heart for them. Wesley states the same in a clause, that Titus was more forward than to need the exhortation, though he received it well.

18.pericope_label: The brother, whose praise is in the gospel, who was also chosen of the churches to travel with us

schools.summary: Barnes reports that it has been generally supposed this anonymous brother was Luke, though some have supposed Mark, others Silas or Barnabas; it is impossible to determine with certainty who it was, nor is it material to know, since whoever it was he was some one well known, in whom the church at Corinth could have entire confidence. Barnes thinks it remarkable that when Paul mentions the man again later in the letter he again does it without specifying his name, and notes as the only circumstance throwing light on the question that Luke was the companion and intimate friend of the Apostle and attended him in his travels. On the second commendation Barnes explains that the man had a new mark of the churches' confidence in being appointed to convey the collection to Jerusalem, many concurring in the choice; and he adds the reason it mattered to Paul, that the Apostle had been unwilling to have charge of the contribution alone and had procured the appointment of someone to undertake it. Ellicott says we cannot get beyond probable conjecture. The general current of patristic interpretation ran in favour of St. Luke, and is represented, he notes, in the Collect for St. Luke's Day in the English Prayer Book though not in the Roman Breviary; but that tradition rested on the assumption, for which there is no evidence and against which there is a strong balance of probabilities, that Luke was already well known as the writer of a Gospel — though apart from that assumption there is still more evidence in favour of the Lucan hypothesis than of any other. On the appointment he takes the word to imply a definite appointment, in this case obviously by popular election on the part of the Macedonian churches, and observes how this falls in with the use of the first person plural in the later chapters of Acts; and on the phrase with this grace he notes that the word is used, as elsewhere in the chapter, much as we familiarly use the word charity, for the liberality which was the result of the grace. Robertson calls the sending an epistolary aorist, and notes that the brother may be, and probably is, Luke, who may also be the brother of Titus by a common Greek idiom in which the article does duty for a possessive — though the idiom is not necessary, and as a matter of fact we do not know who this brother is. On the appointment he explains that the verb is from the stretching out of the hands and so to vote in public, the point being that this brother was chosen by the churches and not by Paul; and he glosses the word for fellow-traveller as a late one meaning one who is away from home together with another.

Clarke lists the candidates without choosing between them: some suppose it was St. Luke, who wrote a gospel and was the companion of St. Paul in several of his travels; others think it was Silas, others Barnabas, others Mark, and others Apollos — neither ancients nor moderns agreeing, though Luke, John and Mark seem to him to have the most probable opinions in their favour. Whoever the person was, Clarke adds, he was sufficiently known to the Corinthians, as we learn from what the Apostle says of him here. On the appointment he derives the verb from the hand and the verb to extend, so that it means appointed by a show of hands, and thinks this appointment by the suffrage of the churches seems to refer more to Luke than to anyone else, unless the reference be to the transaction in Acts where Silas is chosen. He notes besides a textual point, that instead of your ready mind almost all the best manuscripts and all the versions read our, which he judges doubtless the true reading. Wesley records the ancient view simply, that the ancients generally supposed this was St. Luke, and takes his praise to be for faithfully dispensing the gospel through all the churches; on the appointment he specifies that it was by the churches of Macedonia, with the gift they were carrying thence to Jerusalem, and that the declaration of a ready mind means that of Paul and his fellow-traveller, ready to be the servants of all.

Calvin observes first what the sending itself signifies, that the fact of persons being sent is evidence that great expectations were entertained respecting the Corinthians, and that it became them to be so much the more attentive to duty, that they might not disappoint the hopes of the Churches. On the identity he alone among these witnesses commits himself against the majority: it is uncertain who this person was, some conjecturing Luke and others Barnabas, but Chrysostom prefers to consider it to have been Barnabas, and Calvin agrees with him, because it appears that by the suffrages of the Churches Barnabas was associated with Paul as a companion. On the following verse Calvin says that by commending the man's ministry the Apostle still farther encourages the Corinthians, since it tends to promote the glory of God and their own kindness of disposition — these two things being so conjoined that the one cannot be given up without the other being proportionally diminished. Gill draws out the same appointment at more length: this brother was famous not only for preaching the Gospel but was also appointed by the joint suffrages of the churches, which were made by the lifting up or stretching out of the hand, as the word here used signifies — and he was chosen not by a few private persons, nor by a single church only, but by several churches together.

20.pericope_label: Avoiding this, that no man should blame us; providing for honest things in the sight of God and of men

schools.summary: Barnes explains the precaution as a deliberate policy: the Apostle intends to prevent any blame from being cast on him in regard to the management of these funds, and for this purpose had refused to have the entire management of them and had secured the appointment of one who had the entire confidence of all the churches, so that no one should have occasion to say that he had appropriated any of it to his own use or contrary to the will of the donors. Barnes adds the reason, that Paul felt how dangerous it is for ministers to have much to do with money matters, and had a very deep impression of the necessity of keeping his own character free from suspicion on this subject. On the maxim which closes the section he notes that the same expression is used elsewhere by the Apostle, though there of how we are to treat those who injure us and here of the right use of property, and takes it for a kind of maxim by which Paul regulated his life, applicable to everything: the word rendered providing means foreseeing or perceiving beforehand, so that we are to make it a matter of previous calculation, a settled plan, a thing attended to of set design, that all our conduct shall be comely and honest. Ellicott says the Apostle gives here the reason why he wished men thus appointed to travel with him: he desired to guard against the suspicion of those who were too ready to suspect, and his companions were to bear witness that the sums he took up with him from the several churches were what had actually been collected — they were to be, practically, auditors of his accounts, a measure of precaution he dwells on again later in the Epistle. On the maxim Ellicott adds what an English reader cannot see but a Greek reader would notice at once, that the words are a quotation from the Greek version of the Proverbs, and finds the citation interesting as showing that even one who was taught by the Spirit, as St. Paul was, could yet find guidance for his daily conduct in the written word; he notes besides that many of the best manuscripts give the first person, for we provide for honest things, as though the Apostle were stating the general principle on which he was acting in this particular instance. Robertson derives the opening participle from an old verb meaning to set or to arrange, so that the sense is arranging this for ourselves, and renders the following clause literally, lest any one blame us; and on the maxim he draws the practical corollary — it is not enough for one's financial accounts to be honourable as God sees them, but they should be so kept that men can understand them also, which he calls a timely warning, since Paul took the utmost pains that no suspicion could be attached to him in this collection.

Gill hears in the opening verb an allusion to mariners, who when sensible of danger steer their course another way in order to shun a rock and secure themselves; and so the apostles, being aware of the censorious spirits of some persons, and to prevent all suspicion of their converting any part of what they had collected to their own private use, sent Titus with it, a man of known probity and integrity, and not by himself only but with another brother, one who had obtained a good report as a minister of the Gospel in all the churches and was appointed to this service not by the apostles but by the churches themselves. On the maxim Gill explains that to provide for honest things is to premeditate, forecast or consider beforehand in the mind things that are good and of good report among men as well as accounted good by God; for it becomes professors of religion, and especially ministers of the Gospel, to be careful not only to exercise a good conscience towards God but so to behave that they may obtain and preserve the good opinion of men — since when they have once lost their credit and reputation among men, their ministry becomes in a great measure useless. Calvin takes the verb in the same nautical sense, of the furling or altering of the sails of a ship to change her course so that she may avoid rocks or other dangers lying in her way, and supports the usage from Plutarch, who employs it of tempests of the mind so severe that they will not allow a man to shift his course or to calm his troubled reason. He suspects the danger was real and local, since there were not wanting, even among the Corinthians, some who would have proceeded so far as to revile if occasion had been allowed them; and the Apostle wished them to know the state of matters that he might shut the mouths of all everywhere. Accordingly, Calvin says, he declares that he is not merely concerned to have a good conscience in the sight of God but also to have a good character among men — designing besides to instruct the Corinthians, and all others, by his example, that in doing what is right the opinion of men is not to be disregarded.

Clarke calls the arrangement a prudent caution: they took care to have witnesses of their conduct, and such as were chosen by the churches themselves, that they might not be suspected of having either embezzled or misapplied their bounty. On the maxim he states the double requirement in a sentence — take care to act so as not only to be clear in the sight of God but also to be clear in the sight of all men, avoiding even the appearance of evil.

22.pericope_label: We have sent with them our brother; whether any do enquire of Titus, he is my partner and fellowhelper

schools.summary: Barnes calls conjecture about the third brother useless: some have supposed Apollos, others Silas, others Timothy, but there are no means of ascertaining who it was, nor is it material, since it was someone in whom Paul had entire confidence and who had evidently been his companion and fellow-labourer. On the phrase about his being more diligent Barnes takes it of one who will now prove himself much more diligent than ever before. On the closing verse he observes that the words any do inquire are not in the original, and that the Greek may mean either if any inquire about Titus or if anything is to be said about Titus — the sense being either that some of the faction at Corinth might be disposed to inquire about the authority of Titus to engage in this work, or that, having said so much in commendation of the persons who went with Titus, it seemed proper to say something in his favour also. Ellicott says that who this second unnamed brother was is again simply matter of conjecture, but makes the fullest case of any of the witnesses, and for a name none of the others raise: of the names connected with St. Paul at this period, that of Tychicus seems to have the greatest balance of probabilities in its favour, since he went up with the Apostle to Jerusalem on this very business and the tone in which Paul speaks of him in the later letters exactly agrees with the language used here, while other epistles give further evidence of his being one of the most trusted of the couriers or messengers of the Apostolic Church. On the closing verse Ellicott notes that there is no verb in the Greek and that its insertion is not required for the English, our common phrase, as to Titus, exactly expressing the meaning; and on the second title he observes that the Greek word is apostles, used here as in one or two other places in a lower sense, and without the article, for delegates of the churches, as the Twelve and Paul and Barnabas were delegates of Christ. Robertson takes the brother to be not Paul's own brother but a brother in Christ, one whom Paul had tested and was willing to trust, possibly Tychicus or Apollos, though we do not know. On the closing verse he notes that no verb is expressed and that inquire must be supplied, that the Apostle endorses Titus up to the hilt as his partner and fellow-worker, and that the messengers are apostles in the general sense of sent ones — sent by the churches and responsible to the churches for the handling of the funds, which he underlines with the remark that financial agents should please observe it.

Gill notices that the number of messengers may itself be significant, since in sending a third person the Apostle conformed to the customs of his nation, or at least agreed with the Jewish canon which requires three persons for the distribution of alms. Calvin gives the ground of the Apostle's confidence in them: he is not afraid of their coming to Corinth proving vain and fruitless, for he has felt beforehand an assured confidence that their embassy will have a happy issue, being so well aware of their fidelity and diligence. The brother whose name he does not mention had felt more eagerly inclined, Calvin explains, partly because he saw that Paul had a good opinion of the Corinthians, partly because he had been encouraged by Titus, and partly because he saw many distinguished men applying themselves to the same business with united efforts — so that one thing only remained, which was that the Corinthians themselves should not fail them. On the closing verse Calvin considers in what sense the messengers are called apostles of the churches, and decides between two senses: either that they had been set apart by God as apostles, or that they had been appointed by the churches to undertake that office, the latter being the more suitable here. They are called also the glory of Christ, he says, for this reason, that as he alone is the glory of believers, so he ought also to be glorified by them in return — and hence all who excel in piety and holiness are his glory, because they have nothing but by Christ's gift.

Clarke guesses at the names, taking the two who go with Titus to be probably Luke and Apollos, and explains the increased diligence from the Corinthians' own improvement: finding that the Apostle has the fullest confidence in their complete reformation and love to him, the brother engages in this business with alacrity and exceeds even his former diligence. On the closing verse Clarke frames it as a set of questions and answers — should it be asked who this Titus is, the answer is that he is my companion and my fellow labourer in reference to you; and should any inquire who these brethren are, the answer is that they are apostles of the churches, and intensely bent on promoting the glory of Christ. Wesley glosses the two titles briefly, that Titus is the Apostle's partner in his cares and labours, and that the brethren are the glory of Christ as being signal instruments of advancing his glory.

24.pericope_label: Wherefore shew ye to them, and before the churches, the proof of your love, and of our boasting

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the added phrase literally, in the face of the churches, and finds in it the Apostle's characteristic method: in adding it, St. Paul appeals, as he has done throughout the chapter, to that natural love of praise which takes its place as a legitimate, though it may be and ought to be a subordinate, motive for the activity of Christian benevolence. The Corinthians were not to consider only what he and Titus and the two brethren would think of them, for the eyes of the churches were upon them — probably Philippi, Thessalonica and Beroea are referred to. The love appealed to is probably their personal regard for the Apostle himself; and with a subtle knowledge of human nature, Ellicott observes, he attacks them as it were on every side, since they have to compete with Macedonia, they have to show their love for their teacher, and they have to sustain the character he has given them. Barnes states the request in practical terms: by a liberal contribution in the cause in which these men are engaged, and for which they have come among you now, furnish the evidence that you love me and the Christian cause, and show that I have not boasted of you in vain — let it now be seen that my boasting was well founded, and that I properly understood your character and your readiness to contribute to the objects of Christian benevolence. Robertson draws the same picture with a sharper edge: a great host is pictured as watching how the Corinthians will treat these duly accredited agents in the collection, and it requires courage, he remarks, to stand by such representatives of great causes before stingy saints; he adds that there is a word here for pastors and deacons who try to protect their churches from the representatives of wider causes.

Calvin distinguishes the two things mentioned in the close: see that our brethren behold your love, and take care that it be not in vain that I have boasted of you. He settles a small point of reference along the way, that the pronoun looks not to the poor but to the messengers of whom mention had been made, who had been sent as ambassadors to the Corinthians; and he notes that the Apostle immediately afterwards subjoins that they would not be the only witnesses, since in consequence of the report given by them a report would go out even to distant Churches. Gill gives the same account of the audiences. Since these were persons of so much note and worth, they ought to be received with great marks of respect and affection, and the Corinthians should take care evidently to make it appear to those who were sent by the churches, and before the churches, or before those who represented the churches — so that it might be known by the churches from whence they came, when the messengers returned with their report, or be evident to the churches in Judea when the liberality should be brought to them.

Clarke reads the closing exhortation as an appeal to their honour: seeing that these are persons every way worthy in themselves, coming to them on so important an occasion and so highly recommended, let them be received affectionately, and let them thus see that the very high character the Apostle has given of the Corinthians is not exaggerated, and that they are as ready in every work of charity as he has stated them to be — act in this, Clarke says, for your honour. He then stands back and assesses the chapter as a piece of persuasion. The whole of this chapter and the following is occupied in exciting the richer followers of Christ to be liberal to the poorer; the obligation of each to be so, the reasons on which that obligation is founded, and the arguments to enforce the obligation from those reasons, are all clearly stated, and most dexterously and forcibly managed — so that these two chapters afford, in his judgment, a perfect model for a Christian minister who is pleading the cause of the poor. Wesley explains in what sense the churches were present at all, namely by their messengers.
